audit.report: Checkout degraded after a killed batch job was restarted by its scheduler, leaving pid 120535 idle in transaction and blocking checkout sessions. Success fell from 53% over 15 seconds to 27% over 30 seconds, risking about $13,493 per minute against a $18,400 per minute run-rate. The Database Guardian proposed terminating batch_replayable_price_sync because it was replayable, interruptible, and no protected settlements were in flight. The Continuity Guardian accepted, the authority authorized, and the executor terminated pid 120535. Verification failed: a new pid 120649 for the same workload still holds locks, checkout success is 29%, and the incident is escalated; the business is not yet recovered.
audit.root_cause: The restarted batch_replayable_price_sync job (pid 120535, later 120649) remained idle in transaction and held locks that blocked checkout sessions.
lessons: For batch_replayable_price_sync, verify the scheduler actually stopped the old process after a kill before assuming the lock is released, since a restarted replayable job can re-acquire the same blocker.
Before terminating any blocker on checkout, confirm no new instance of batch_replayable_price_sync has started and re-check lock waiters within the 60-second degradation tolerance.
Track replay cost and runtime for batch_replayable_price_sync (2-minute replay, ~600s typical) so the next negotiation can compare termination cost against waiting cost in the same round.
audit.negotiation_critique: The guardians reached agreement in one round with complete evidence, but neither anticipated that terminating pid 120535 would not clear the locks because the scheduler restarted the same workload as pid 120649.
follow_ups: Terminate pid 120649 and confirm database_clear before declaring recovery.
Investigate why the scheduler restarted batch_replayable_price_sync after it was killed and prevent automatic restart during checkout incidents.
